extracted.intended_audience: patent practitioners, judges, and law students (those drafting, litigating, or interpreting patent specifications and claims)
extracted.subtask_description: Principles and legal standards for drafting and construing patent specifications and claims: what must be disclosed, how claims must be framed (not as abstract principles or mere results), enablement, and the proper scope of claims applying a principle to practical effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Specification must fully explain the principle and the several modes
rubrics_metrics.description: The specification must 'fully explain the principle and the several modes in which he has contemplated the application of that principle ... and shall particularly specify and point out the part, improvement, or combination, which he claims as his own invention or discovery.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The 'principle' means the peculiar structure and mode of operation or the character by which the invention may be distinguished. The patentee should state not only the preferred device or construction but also the other modes of applying the principle he intends to claim; however, he need not enter into minute descriptions of every variation — it is sufficient to indicate what variations of application he claims beyond the preferred embodiments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not claim an abstract principle; show a practical application
rubrics_metrics.description: A patentee cannot appropriate a mere abstract principle, idea, or function; the specification must give the discovery a practical application to some useful purpose by its incorporation with matter so as to produce a practical result.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the invention is only stated as an abstract philosophical principle or law of nature, it is not patentable. But if the principle is applied to a special purpose so as to effectuate a practical and previously unknown result, the patent can be valid. (Illustrated by the Househill/Neilson discussion: a general principle stated plus an application to a special purpose becomes a 'practical invention'.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Claims must recite the means/apparatus, not merely a result
rubrics_metrics.description: A claim that is effectively a claim for a result or function without identifying the means by which it is produced will not be sustained; the claim must be for the means or apparatus by which the result is produced.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: a claim to the use of proper chemicals to precipitate metal from a solution, by putting such chemicals into any proper vessel, was held too general and vague and therefore invalid. Claims should identify the operative means/structure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Enablement: specification must be full and exact for skilled person
rubrics_metrics.description: The patentee must 'specify the means used in a manner so full and exact that any one skilled in the science ... can, by using the means he specifies, without any addition to or subtraction from them, produce precisely the result he describes.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the skilled practitioner cannot produce the result by the means described, the patent is void. The patentee's exclusive right extends to the means he specifies to produce the described effect and nothing more.

rubrics_metrics.name: For machines, patent the machine (embodiment), not a bare mode or idea
rubrics_metrics.description: Where the invention falls within 'machines', the patent must be for the machine itself and not for a 'mode of operation,' 'principle,' 'idea,' or other abstraction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Claims framed as the specific machine or its organization (mode of operation embodied in particular structure) will be sustained, whereas claims sweeping all possible modes of operation are void. Court examples show courts construing such patents as for the described machine when the specification points to a particular structure.

rubrics_metrics.name: A new application of a natural property can be patented even without new machinery
rubrics_metrics.description: When a party discovers a new application of some property in nature that produces a new and useful result, the discovery is patentable independent of any peculiar or new arrangement of machinery for applying it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The inventor may use any means, old or new, to apply the new property; the patent excludes others from using those means and other means in a similar application. (Cases like Foote v. Silsby and Neilson discussed.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Combination claims cover the specific combination, not all modes of combining
rubrics_metrics.description: A claim for a combination of several devices is a claim for that combination as described, and is not a valid claim for any and all modes of combining such devices.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts will sustain a claim only as to the particular combination or the machine specially described; they will not permit a combination claim to function as a universal claim to any mode achieving the result.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claims referring back to the specification ('substantially as described') are construed in light of the spec
rubrics_metrics.description: A claim containing words referring back to the specifications (e.g., 'substantially as described' or 'substantially as set forth') must be construed in connection with the specification and may be held valid when so construed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where a claim immediately follows the descriptive part of the specification, courts will read the claim in the context of that description rather than isolate the claim language.

rubrics_metrics.name: Variations of means that produce the same application may still infringe
rubrics_metrics.description: Although the patentee must describe some machinery or practical method to show he has applied the principle, a variation of the means or machinery that produces the same beneficial effect (i.e., the same application of the same principle) may still constitute infringement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Thus the patentee's subject-matter can embrace different forms of apparatus that effect the same application of the principle (illustrated by Neilson's hot-blast furnace patent covering various shapes of heating receptacles).

rubrics_metrics.name: A claim broader than its specification is invalid
rubrics_metrics.description: If a claim 'stands outside' or extends beyond the specification — i.e., the claim's broad terms are not supported by the specification — the claim is invalid.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Famous example: the broad eighth claim in O'Reilly v. Morse, which claimed the use of electromagnetic force to print characters 'at any distance' beyond the specification, was held invalid. Claims cannot derive substance from bare broad terms unsupported by the spec.

rubrics_metrics.name: Courts must construe the specification to determine whether the claim is for a patentable subject
rubrics_metrics.description: Determining what the patentee's claim is requires construing the description in the specification to see whether it discloses a patentable subject (a particular organization of matter/machine) or merely a function/abstract principle.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The real invention may be patentable, but if claimed as an abstract principle or function, courts will declare it not patentable; the specification's form of description can change a claim from impermissible abstraction into a patentable applied invention if it shows the application to a special purpose.
